title: Shape the soul
hook: philosophy isn't a show of words; it shapes and builds the soul

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Salian priests, whose hopping dance made Seneca's short list of exercise. Your line was brief for the body.

Some people can quote a whole shelf of self-help books and still lose their temper in a parking lot. Others have never read a page of philosophy and are the steadiest person in any room. Knowing and living don't always travel together. Four hundred and fifty days into this path, there are a fair number of good lines behind you. Seneca's sixteenth letter asks the uncomfortable question: what are they actually doing?
screen: `QUOTES THE BOOK, LOSES IT IN TRAFFIC.` → `KNOWING ISN'T LIVING.` → `SHAPE THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: It's not enough to have made good resolutions, Seneca tells Lucilius. Keeping them takes more work than making them. You have to strengthen them every day, until good intention becomes settled character. Then he says it plainly. Philosophy isn't a trick for the crowd, or something to show off, or a way to pass the time and chase away boredom. In the Latin: non in verbis, sed in rebus. Not in words, but in deeds. It shapes and builds the soul, he says. It puts life in order, guides what you do, and shows you what to take up and what to leave. It sits at the helm and steers us through the waves. A soul isn't handed to you finished. It gets formed, like clay on a wheel, by what you do over and over. Someone might object: what good is all this, if fate rules everything, or God, or blind chance? Seneca's answer: whichever is true, we still have to live, and philosophy is what helps us bear it well. Then he signs off with a gift from Epicurus: live by nature and you'll never be poor; live by opinion and you'll never be rich. So the test of four hundred fifty days isn't how many lines you can quote. It's whether one of them has changed what your hands do on a Tuesday.
screen: `KEEPING RESOLUTIONS TAKES WORK.` · `NOT IN WORDS, BUT IN DEEDS.` · `IT SHAPES THE SOUL, STEERS THE SHIP.` · `FATE, GOD OR CHANCE: STILL LIVE WELL.` · then, large: `NOT WORDS, SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Say to yourself, in a few words, one thing you truly believe about how to live, from this path or from your own family or faith. Ask, without scolding, where you acted on it this week and where you didn't. Then picture one small act that would put that belief into your hands instead of your head.
Epicurus. The line Seneca borrows to close this letter: live by nature and you'll never be poor; live by opinion and you'll never be rich. Today's word.
Your line: not words, shape. Deeds, done over and over, form the soul. Four hundred fifty days now.

screen: `DAY 450 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T WAIT TO BE RICH.`

howItsDone: For Stoics, philosophy is measured by conduct: people who practice it try to turn a belief into one concrete action each day, and to renew their resolutions daily.
